The Election of 1824. When no candidate won an Electoral College majority, this election was thrown into the House of Representatives, resulting in the controversial selection of John Quincy Adams over the popular-vote leader Andrew Jackson. The so-called Corrupt Bargain—alleged collusion between Adams and Henry Clay to hand the presidency to Adams—sparked outrage and fractured the Democratic-Republican Party.

Andrew Jackson led with ninety-nine electoral votes and forty-two percent of the popular vote, but fell short of a majority. John Quincy Adams, William Crawford, and Henry Clay followed; only the top three could advance to the House vote under the Twelfth Amendment. Clay's elimination, despite his formidable stature, left him free to influence the House, a position he capitalized on brilliantly.

The House chose Adams over Jackson in one ballot, with Clay's crucial support from the Kentucky delegation. Jackson supporters claimed a backroom deal: Adams would win the presidency and Clay would become Secretary of State—and indeed, Clay accepted that post. The Bargain became the defining scandal of Adams's term, poisoning his presidency before it began.

Jackson's partisans mobilized for 1828, vowing to overturn the stolen election and launching the Democratic Party as a distinct faction. Adams's one term was marked by legislative paralysis; he could accomplish little against a hostile, Jackson-allied Congress. The election exposed the inadequacy of the Electoral College system and became the rallying cry for Jacksonian democracy. Andrew Jackson would be the apparent victor who was denied, sparking his successful 1828 campaign.
